title: Chapter 2 — The Carpet-Bag
paragraphs: I stuffed a shirt or two into my old carpet-bag, tucked it under my arm, and headed for Cape Horn and the Pacific. Leaving the good city of old Manhattan, I arrived in New Bedford. It was a Saturday night in December. I was very disappointed to learn that the little packet boat to Nantucket had already sailed, and there was no way to get there until Monday.

Since most young candidates for the punishments of whaling stop in this same New Bedford before embarking, I should mention that I had no intention of doing the same. I was determined to sail on a Nantucket ship, because there was something fine and wild about everything connected with that famous old island that pleased me enormously. Besides, though New Bedford has gradually been taking over the whaling business, and poor old Nantucket now trails far behind, Nantucket was the original — the Tyre to New Bedford's Carthage, the place where the first dead American whale washed ashore. Where else but Nantucket did those original whalemen, the Native Americans, first paddle out in canoes to chase the great beast? And where else did that first small, daring sloop set sail, partly loaded — so the story goes — with cobblestones to throw at whales, to judge when they were close enough to risk a harpoon?

Now, facing a night, a day, and another night in New Bedford before I could set out for my destination, the question of where to eat and sleep became pressing. It was a grim-looking night — dark, dismal, bitingly cold, and cheerless. I knew no one in the place. I'd anxiously searched my pocket and found only a few silver coins. So, wherever you go, Ishmael, I said to myself, standing in the middle of a dreary street with my bag on my shoulder, comparing the gloom to the north with the darkness to the south — wherever you decide to sleep tonight, my dear Ishmael, be sure to ask the price, and don't be too picky.

With halting steps I walked the streets and passed the sign of 'The Crossed Harpoons' — but it looked too expensive and festive in there. Further on, from the bright red windows of the 'Sword-Fish Inn,' such warm light poured out that it seemed to have melted the packed snow in front of the building, while everywhere else the frozen ground lay ten inches thick like hard pavement. Rough going for me, striking my foot against the flinty ridges, since my boot soles were in miserable shape from hard service. Too expensive and festive again, I thought, pausing to watch the bright glow in the street and hear the clinking glasses inside. But move along, Ishmael, I told myself at last — don't you hear? Get away from the door; your patched boots are blocking the way. So on I went, instinctively following streets that led me toward the water, where the cheapest — if not the cheeriest — inns were sure to be.

What dreary streets! Solid blocks of blackness, not houses, on either side, and here and there a candle, like a flame moving in a tomb. At this hour of night, on the last day of the week, that part of town was all but deserted. But soon I came to a dim, smoky light from a low, wide building with its door standing invitingly open. It had a careless look, as if it were meant for public use. I walked in and immediately stumbled over an ash-box in the entrance. Ha! I thought, choking on the flying particles — are these ashes from that destroyed city, Gomorrah? But 'The Crossed Harpoons' and 'The Sword-Fish'? Then this must be the sign of 'The Trap.'

It looked like some great dark parliament sitting in Hell. A hundred dark faces turned in their rows to stare, and beyond them, a dark figure was pounding a book in a pulpit. It was a Black church, and the preacher's text was about the blackness of darkness, the weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth. Ha, Ishmael, I muttered, backing out — what wretched entertainment at the sign of 'The Trap'!

Moving on, I eventually came to a faint light not far from the docks and heard a forlorn creaking in the air. Looking up, I saw a swinging sign over a door with a white painting on it, faintly depicting a tall, straight jet of misty spray, and these words underneath: 'The Spouter Inn: — Peter Coffin.'

Coffin? Spouter? Rather ominous in that particular combination, I thought. But it's a common name in Nantucket, they say, and I suppose this Peter is originally from there. Since the light was dim, the place seemed quiet enough, and the dilapidated little wooden house looked as if it might have been carted here from the ruins of some burned district — and since the swinging sign had a poverty-stricken creak to it — I figured this was exactly the spot for cheap lodgings and decent coffee.

It was an odd sort of place — a gable-ended old house, one side almost paralyzed, leaning over sadly. It stood on a sharp, bleak corner where the tempestuous northeast wind howled worse than it ever did around poor Saint Paul's storm-tossed ship. But that same wind is a perfectly pleasant breeze if you're indoors with your feet on the hearth, getting ready for bed. 'In judging of that tempestuous wind called Euroclydon,' says an old writer whose works only I possess, 'it makes a marvelous difference whether you look at it from a glass window with the frost all on the outside, or from a sashless window where the frost is on both sides, and Death is the only glazier.' True enough, I thought — old black-letter, you reason well. Yes, these eyes are windows, and this body of mine is the house. What a shame they didn't seal up the cracks and stuff in some insulation. But it's too late for improvements now. The universe is finished; the capstone is on, and the scraps were hauled away a million years ago. Poor Lazarus there, chattering his teeth against the curbstone as his pillow, shaking off his rags with his shivering — he might plug both ears with scraps and stick a corncob in his mouth, and still the freezing wind would find him. 'Euroclydon!' says old Dives in his red silk robe — he'd have a redder one later — 'Bah! What a fine frosty night! How Orion glitters! What northern lights! Let them talk about their tropical conservatories — give me the privilege of making my own summer with my own coals.'

But what does Lazarus think? Can he warm his blue hands by holding them up to the northern lights? Wouldn't Lazarus rather be in Sumatra than here? Wouldn't he far rather stretch himself out along the equator — or even descend to the fiery pit itself — just to escape this frost?

Now, that Lazarus should lie stranded on the curb outside the door of Dives — this is more astonishing than an iceberg moored to a tropical island. Yet Dives himself lives like a czar in an ice palace made of frozen sighs, and being president of a temperance society, he drinks only the lukewarm tears of orphans.
But enough of this blubbering — we're going whaling, and there's plenty of that to come. Let's scrape the ice from our frozen feet and see what kind of place this 'Spouter' is.
